async_compute_overlap.problem: A frame rendered purely on the graphics queue leaves GPU resources idle: fixed-function-heavy passes (shadow rasterisation, depth-only) do not saturate the shader cores, and barriers drain the queues. Async compute moves independent work onto a second queue to fill those gaps.

implementation_variants.name: Move the post-processing compute chain to a second queue
implementation_variants.description: Khronos' official sample measures this directly: 'Here we can see a nice perf win (21.8 ms vs. 22.9 ms), and fragment cycles is very close to GPU cycles now, which means no starvation is happening.' The win comes from removing a COMPUTE -> FRAGMENT barrier that blocked the fragment queue.

implementation_variants.name: Overlap the post-processing of frame N with the shadow rendering of frame N+1
implementation_variants.description: AMD's recommended pattern: 'A common solution for efficient asynchronous compute usage can be to overlap the post processing of frame N with shadow map rendering of frame N+1.'

implementation_variants.name: Use a depth-only pass as the overlap host
implementation_variants.description: AMD: 'Depth only rendering passes are usually good candidates to have some compute tasks run next to it.' The sample's own scenario exploits 'the shadow mapping pass, which is extremely bound on fixed function rasterization performance'.

implementation_variants.name: Copy/transfer queue for streaming, double-buffered
implementation_variants.description: AMD's concrete shipped result: without double buffering 'using the copy queue did not result in any performance advantage'; after double buffering 'the upload now happens while the previous frame is still being processed ... This change saved almost 10% of the total frame time.'

implementation_variants.name: Render graph with automatic async-compute fences and split barriers
implementation_variants.description: Making overlap the default rather than a hand-tuned special case: the graph knows the resource dependencies, so it can insert the fences and split barriers itself and cull unused passes.

async_compute_overlap.applicability_conditions: Requires a modern explicit API (D3D12/Vulkan) and a pass structure where at least two passes have complementary bottlenecks. AMD: 'it is recommended to determine bottlenecks for each pass and place passes with complementary bottlenecks next to each other.'
async_compute_overlap.limitations: Queues share the GPU. AMD lists four ways this bites: system-memory resources contend with the DMA queue; local-memory/bandwidth-heavy work on both queues contend; 'Threads sharing the same CU will share GPRs and LDS'; and 'Different queues share their caches ... more cache thrashing'. AMD states plainly: 'asynchronous compute can reduce performance when not used optimally.' On GCN, multiple direct queues gain nothing ('GCN hardware contains a single geometry frontend'), and AMD 'haven't seen significant performance benefits from using more than one compute queue'. On TBDR GPUs a COMPUTE -> FRAGMENT barrier is a documented 'Perf cliff'. Command lists must also be big enough: 'make sure each command list is big enough' to pay for 'the cost of splitting the command list and stalling on fences'.
async_compute_overlap.required_data_and_tools: GPUView (AMD's recommendation) or an IHV profiler that can visualise per-queue saturation, plus the ability to toggle async per task so A/B measurements are possible. Khronos: 'It is important to note that asynchronous compute can reduce performance when not used optimally ... make sure asynchronous compute usage can easily be enabled or disabled for each task.'

impact.cpu: low to medium (more command lists to build and submit; more fences)
impact.gpu: medium potential reduction of frame time; measured 21.8 ms vs 22.9 ms in the Khronos sample and 'almost 10%' of total frame time in AMD's copy-queue example
impact.vram: low to medium (double-buffering resources costs memory)

async_compute_overlap.quality_impact: None when correct. Incorrect fencing produces race artefacts, which is why the technique must be toggleable.
async_compute_overlap.concept_impact: Recovers otherwise-unused GPU capacity; enables expensive compute passes (GI, volumetrics, post) that would not fit sequentially.
async_compute_overlap.recommended_stage: vertical_slice_or_later, after the frame has a stable pass structure. Doing it earlier means re-tuning every time the graph changes.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 4d graph/queue infrastructure + 6d candidate-pass selection and fencing + 8d A/B measurement per platform (AMD explicitly requires per-task on/off toggles and per-hardware validation); p80 = round(1.6 * p50)

relations.note: AMD: 'we recommend to implement a compute path for as many render workloads as possible in order to have more freedom in determining which tasks to overlap'.
GPU occlusion culling is a natural compute-queue workload, and it enables the geometry savings that make the rest of the frame cheaper.
Volumetrics are compute-heavy and depend only on depth - a textbook async candidate.
Splitting the frame across queues multiplies the number of PSOs that must be warm.
Async behaviour is hardware-specific; a tier that assumes overlap on desktop may regress on mobile TBDR.

async_compute_overlap.verification: One scene with async on/off: capture the GPU timeline, compare p95/p99 frame time and latency, run validation layers, and confirm no visual delta.

bindless_uber_shaders.problem: Traditional binding forces a descriptor/state change per material, which caps how aggressively draws can be merged and explodes the shader-permutation count. Bindless resources plus a small number of uber shaders remove both limits.

implementation_variants.name: Direct heap indexing in HLSL (Shader Model 6.6)
implementation_variants.description: 'In HLSL, two new builtin global indexable objects allow you to set local resource and sampler objects by directly indexing into the CBV_SRV_UAV (Resource) descriptor heap or the Sampler descriptor heap.' Requires the root signature flags CBV_SRV_UAV_HEAP_DIRECTLY_INDEXED (0x400) and/or SAMPLER_HEAP_DIRECTLY_INDEXED (0x800), and 'must be supported on devices that support both D3D12_RESOURCE_BINDING_TIER_3 and D3D_SHADER_MODEL_6_6'.

implementation_variants.name: Bindless texture table + unified vertex buffer (id Tech 7)
implementation_variants.description: 'instead of binding e.g. a diffuse, specular, roughness, ... textures before every draw call, the entire list of textures in the scene is bound at once. The textures in the list are accessed dynamically in the shader by means of indices'. Combined with 'all geometry data ... allocated from a single large buffer/pool' where 'All geometry simply has an offset in this buffer'.

implementation_variants.name: Uber shaders to collapse the permutation explosion
implementation_variants.description: 'Almost all materials and features are combined into very few massive "uber shaders". This allows the graphics pipeline to merge geometry more aggressively which can significantly improve performance.' Unity gives the same advice from the CPU side: 'If you did a lot of different Shaders, try to make a "uber" one with more parameters. Having tons of different material parameters is then free.'

implementation_variants.name: Dynamic draw-call merging built on top of bindless
implementation_variants.description: 'a compute shader dynamically creates a new "indirect" index buffer to effectively merge geometry from unrelated meshes into a single indirect draw call. This would never be achievable without bindless resources because this draw call merging can work across geometry that doesn't share the same material properties.' The merged index buffer is reused for the depth prepass and the lighting pass.

bindless_uber_shaders.applicability_conditions: Requires SM 6.6 + Resource Binding Tier 3 on D3D12, or descriptor indexing on Vulkan; and requires the renderer to be able to keep the whole scene's texture set resident (streaming must not thrash the heap).
bindless_uber_shaders.limitations: Descriptors and their data 'must be considered volatile', which forfeits driver optimisations available to statically-bound resources. Non-uniform indices require NonUniformResourceIndex ('If the index is not uniform and NonUniformResourceIndex is not used, The result may be undefined'). The flags 'are not allowed on local root signatures', so raytracing hit groups cannot use them that way. There is also a new ordering constraint: SetDescriptorHeaps must precede the Set*RootSignature call that uses the flags. In id Tech's case the decal-ID approach itself is capped: 'the maximum amount of decals per mesh would theoretically be 255'.
bindless_uber_shaders.required_data_and_tools: A bindless descriptor heap manager, a material parameter buffer indexed by draw/instance, and a frame-capture tool to count draws and state changes (the catalog's own verification method).

impact.cpu: high reduction in submission/state-change cost (this is where the win is)
impact.gpu: low to medium (fewer state changes, better batching; uber shaders can cost register occupancy)
impact.vram: low to medium (whole-scene descriptor heap and resident texture set)

bindless_uber_shaders.quality_impact: Neutral to positive: fewer permutation limits means artists can vary materials freely; the risk is that an uber shader grows so large that it hurts occupancy.
bindless_uber_shaders.concept_impact: Prerequisite for aggressive GPU-driven rendering: without bindless, geometry with different materials cannot be merged into one indirect draw.
bindless_uber_shaders.recommended_stage: preproduction - bindless is an architectural commitment. Retro-fitting it into a renderer built around per-draw descriptor tables is a rewrite, not a patch.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 10d descriptor-heap/material-parameter infrastructure + 8d shader-port to SM6.6 with NonUniformResourceIndex audit + 7d uber-shader consolidation + 10d validation across vendors; p80 = round(1.6 * p50). No published effort figure; expert_estimate.

relations.note: The CPU-side analogue: both approaches reduce per-draw setup by making material data persistent and by minimising shader-variant changes. Unity: 'In SRP Batcher context, the SetShaderPass is called for each new shader variant.'
Collapsing permutations with uber shaders is the cheapest way to shrink the PSO precache problem; id Tech 7 reportedly ships 'about ~500 pipeline states and a dozen descriptor layouts'.
Both are parts of the same GPU-driven pipeline; mesh shading removes the index-buffer barrier and bindless removes the material barrier to merging draws.
AMD: 'we recommend to implement a compute path for as many render workloads as possible' - bindless makes that practical.

bindless_uber_shaders.verification: Count draws and pipeline/descriptor state changes in a frame capture before and after; report descriptor statistics; confirm no validation-layer errors and no visual delta.

hiz_software_occlusion.problem: Frustum culling alone cannot remove geometry hidden behind other geometry. Occlusion queries stall the CPU; a GPU-side hierarchical depth test removes hidden draws without a round trip.

implementation_variants.name: Hi-Z pyramid built from the depth buffer, tested with a 2x2 fetch
implementation_variants.description: 'After rendering all the occluders in the scene, we construct a hierarchical depth image from the depth buffer ... a mip-mapped, screen resolution image where each texel in mip level i contains the maximum depth of all corresponding texels in mip level i-1.' LOD is chosen so the bounds cover ~2x2 texels: 'float LOD = ceil(log2(max(ViewSizeX, ViewSizeY) / 2.0));', then 'we simply have to make four texture lookups ... calculate the maximum of the four depth values ... If the object depth is greater than the reference depth the object is occluded'.

implementation_variants.name: Two-phase: previous-frame depth first, current-frame confirmation
implementation_variants.description: Reproject last frame's depth to get a conservative visible set immediately, then refine against the current frame's Hi-Z. Removes most of the 'occluders must already be drawn' ordering constraint at the cost of one-frame latency on newly revealed objects.

implementation_variants.name: Meshlet / cluster-level occlusion in a GPU-driven pipeline
implementation_variants.description: Remedy's Northlight is documented as using 'a new GPU-driven rendering pipeline' with 'mesh shaders' giving 'single-pixel occlusion precision' and 'meshlet culling'. This moves the test from per-object to per-meshlet, which is where the win is for dense geometry.

implementation_variants.name: Software rasteriser on the CPU for a small occluder set
implementation_variants.description: Rasterise a coarse occluder set into a low-resolution depth buffer on the CPU and test bounds against it. Useful when the GPU is the bottleneck and CPU threads are free; needs a strict occluder budget.

hiz_software_occlusion.applicability_conditions: The scene must actually contain occlusion (interiors, cities, dense foliage). It requires depth from the current frame (or a reprojected previous frame) before the test can run, and it needs a coarse bounding volume per cullable unit.
hiz_software_occlusion.limitations: The result is conservative, not exact: 'The algorithm presented in this article is somewhat even more conservative but enables the use of occlusion culling for much larger datasets' - it returns 'not visible' or 'most probably visible'. Occluder depth must exist first ('After rendering all the occluders in the scene, we construct a hierarchical depth image'), which for MSAA requires 'a separate full-screen quad pass'. Searching for more culling effectiveness stops paying: 'it is possible to use more complex screen space bounding polygon as well as more fetches but those would increase the effectiveness of the culling much less than the additional burden'. And a single-fetch variant is counter-productive: 'it is possible that we have to fetch the largest LOD ... it severely degrades the effectiveness of the culling'.
hiz_software_occlusion.required_data_and_tools: A depth buffer you can build mips from, a per-object/per-meshlet bounds buffer, and a GPU profiler or frame capture to measure overdraw before/after.

impact.cpu: low to medium reduction in submission work (fewer draws issued)
impact.gpu: low (Hi-Z construction quoted at 'less than 0.2 milliseconds' on a Radeon HD5770) with a medium reduction in vertex/raster work for occluded geometry
impact.vram: low (one depth mip chain; the reference map is 1024x768 in the article's figure)

hiz_software_occlusion.quality_impact: None when conservative. Aggressive (non-conservative) variants pop geometry in, which is why the conservative formulation is standard.
hiz_software_occlusion.concept_impact: Lets levels be authored with heavy occlusion without paying for it, and is a prerequisite for GPU-driven rendering where the CPU no longer decides visibility.
hiz_software_occlusion.recommended_stage: vertical_slice, once there is representative level density. Culling tuned on an empty test map will be mis-tuned for the real game.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 5d Hi-Z build + 4d cull pass and integration into the visibility system + 4d correctness/debugging (conservative bounds, one-frame latency artefacts) + 3d measurement; p80 = round(1.6 * p50). Excludes a full GPU-driven rewrite.

Remedy's GPU-driven pipeline combines mesh shaders with 'meshlet culling' and 'single-pixel occlusion precision'.
Occlusion culling is a compute workload that overlaps well with depth-only rasterisation.
Volumetric fog needs depth for every pixel, so aggressively culled geometry can produce shadows/fog that disagree with the visible set.

pso_precaching_warmup.problem: On D3D12/Vulkan/Metal a pipeline state object must be created before a draw can use it. Creating it during gameplay costs a hitch long enough to be visible.

implementation_variants.name: Offline PSO cache collection, shipped with the build
implementation_variants.description: Epic states the cost being avoided: 'Generating PSOs on demand can take 100 or more milliseconds'. The documented workflow is a manual pass over the game that records every PSO into a cache file, followed by a bundling step.

implementation_variants.name: Warmup screen / loading pass that forces the states
implementation_variants.description: Render the required permutations once during a loading screen so the hitch is hidden inside a load. Requires knowing the permutation set in advance, which is the hard part.

implementation_variants.name: Shrink the permutation set with uber shaders
implementation_variants.description: The cheapest PSO is the one that does not exist. id Tech 7 reportedly ships 'about ~500 pipeline states and a dozen descriptor layouts'; Unity gives the same guidance: 'Try to reduce the number of Shader variants ... try to make a "uber" one with more parameters. Having tons of different material parameters is then free.'

implementation_variants.name: Background/async compilation with a fallback state
implementation_variants.description: Compile on a worker thread and draw with a simpler state until the real one is ready. Removes the hitch but transiently changes shading, so it must be visually acceptable.

pso_precaching_warmup.applicability_conditions: Applies to any renderer on an explicit API (D3D12, Vulkan, Metal). The more material/feature permutations the content uses, the larger the problem.
pso_precaching_warmup.limitations: Epic notes 'Caching of Ray Tracing PSOs is not supported in UE 5.0'. A cache is only as complete as the coverage run that produced it: any permutation first seen in live gameplay still hitches. Shrinking permutations with uber shaders trades PSO count for register pressure.
pso_precaching_warmup.required_data_and_tools: A PSO recording/caching tool plus a bundling step, a coverage run over all levels and all quality tiers, and a hitch detector (frame-time spike logging) during first traversal of the world.

impact.cpu: high reduction in worst-case frame spikes (this is a latency fix, not a throughput fix)
impact.gpu: none
impact.disk: low to medium (the cache file ships with the build)

pso_precaching_warmup.quality_impact: None when the cache is complete. Async-compilation fallbacks can cause a brief visual change.
pso_precaching_warmup.concept_impact: Removes a class of 'random hitch' bugs that are otherwise extremely hard to reproduce and attribute.
pso_precaching_warmup.recommended_stage: vertical_slice and continuously thereafter - the cache must be regenerated whenever content or shaders change, and validated on every platform.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 3d cache pipeline setup + 5d coverage run across levels and tiers + 3d automation in the build + 3d hitch validation; p80 = round(1.6 * p50). Recurring cost per content milestone is not included.

relations.note: Fewer shader permutations means a smaller PSO set to precache; Unity's advice is explicitly to build an 'uber' shader with more parameters.
Both are about minimising shader-variant switches: 'In SRP Batcher context, the SetShaderPass is called for each new shader variant.'
Epic states RT PSOs could not be cached in UE 5.0, so RT features reintroduce exactly the hitch this method removes.
Each quality tier is a different permutation set; the coverage run must visit all of them.

pso_precaching_warmup.verification: Hitch detection on a first traversal of the world: log frame-time spikes over a threshold, trace load/compile events, and confirm zero PSO creations after the warmup completes.

srp_batcher_discipline.problem: In a scene with many different materials, the classic Unity render loop re-uploads material data and re-runs SetShaderPass for every material change, so CPU rendering time scales with material count rather than with what actually needs to change.

implementation_variants.name: SRP Batcher: persistent material CBUFFERs + a large per-object CBUFFER
implementation_variants.description: 'low-level render loops can make material data persistent in the GPU memory. If the Material content does not change, there is no need to set up and upload the buffer to the GPU.' The speedup comes from two things: 'Each material content is now persistent in GPU memory' and 'A dedicated code is managing a large "per object" GPU CBUFFER'.

implementation_variants.name: CBUFFER discipline: UnityPerDraw + UnityPerMaterial
implementation_variants.description: 'All built-in engine properties must be declared in a single CBUFFER named "UnityPerDraw"' and 'All Material properties must be declared in a single CBUFFER named "UnityPerMaterial"'. The UnityPerDraw layout must follow the documented 'Block Feature' ordering.

implementation_variants.name: Minimise shader variants so batches stay long
implementation_variants.description: 'In SRP Batcher context, the SetShaderPass is called for each new shader variant.' Batches break on keyword changes - the Frame Debugger reports the cause, e.g. 'Node use different shader keywords'. Guidance: 'try to write generic "uber" shader with minimum keywords'.

implementation_variants.name: Keep incompatible primitive types off the hot path
implementation_variants.description: Compatibility requires 'The object must be in a mesh. It cannot be a particle or a skinned mesh.' In the FPS Sample benchmark, 'there is still 1.67ms going to the standard code path because of SRP Batcher incompatibility. In this case, skinned meshes and a few particles rendered using Material Property Blocks.'

srp_batcher_discipline.applicability_conditions: Requires LWRP/HDRP or a custom SRP, and shaders written to the CBUFFER rules. Unity: 'To activate the SRP Batcher in HDRP or LWRP, just use the checkbox in the SRP Asset Inspector.' VR is supported only in SinglePassInstanced mode.
srp_batcher_discipline.limitations: It does not reduce draw calls: 'SRP Batcher doesn't reduce the number of DrawCalls. It just reduces the GPU setup cost between DrawCalls.' It is a CPU-side win only - in the Book of the Dead benchmark 'FPS doesn't change, because this scene is GPU bound'. Particles and skinned meshes fall back to the standard path, and Material Property Blocks break batching. The measured spread is wide: '1.2x to 4x, depending on the Scene'.
srp_batcher_discipline.required_data_and_tools: SRPBatcherProfiler.cs (F8 overlay, F9 on/off toggle) to separate 'SRP Batcher code path' from 'Standard code path' time, and the Frame Debugger to inspect 'SRP Batch' event lengths and the reason a batch was broken.

impact.cpu: high reduction in render-thread CPU time (measured 1.2x-4x depending on scene; 6.8 ms saved in Unity's worst-case demo scene)
impact.gpu: none (explicitly: 'we're not talking about global framerate (FPS)')
impact.vram: low to medium (persistent material CBUFFERs are resident)

srp_batcher_discipline.quality_impact: None. It is a pure CPU-cost change.
srp_batcher_discipline.concept_impact: Lets artists use many distinct materials without paying CPU per material, which removes a common art/tech constraint.
srp_batcher_discipline.recommended_stage: vertical_slice, then continuously: shader compatibility has to be checked every time a shader is added ('always check the compatibility status of a new shader in the inspector').

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 2d enable + 3d shader CBUFFER audit and fixes + 3d profiler-driven variant reduction + 2d regression check; p80 = round(1.6 * p50). Covers adopting the discipline, not writing a custom SRP.

Fewer variants means fewer PSOs to precache.
Independent axes (CPU submission vs GPU light assignment); no source found that measures them together.

tiled_clustered_light_culling.problem: Deferred shading pays a per-pixel cost proportional to the number of lights that affect the pixel's neighbourhood. Without culling, cost grows with total light count instead of with lights actually visible.

implementation_variants.name: Clustered shading (32x32 screen tiles x exponential view-space depth slices)
implementation_variants.description: The canonical paper subdivides the frustum in 3D: screen tiles of 32x32 pixels plus exponential depth subdivision, then assigns lights per cluster. Reported figures: '~2400 light sources ... rendered in 17ms', with '2.3ms for clustering, 1.5ms for light assignment and 5.6ms for shading'.

implementation_variants.name: Tiled forward / forward+
implementation_variants.description: Same screen-tile idea without the depth subdivision. The paper's comparison: 'Deferred takes a total of 97.1 ms, and TiledForward 23.6 ms' for the same scene. Tiled wins at low light counts but degrades as lights grow: at 32 lights '0.71 ms' (clustered) vs '0.24 ms' (tiled), while at 32768 lights it is '1.42 ms' vs '9.31 ms'.

implementation_variants.name: Hybrid cluster + tile list selection (id Tech 7)
implementation_variants.description: Build both lists and let the shader pick: 'LIGHT LIST SELECTION - Each fragment invocation checks both its cluster and tile and selects list with fewer entries'. The whole binning pass is held to 'Very tight budget (<500us)'.

implementation_variants.name: Compute-based light assignment with min/max depth bounds per cluster
implementation_variants.description: The standard modern form: build the cluster list in a compute pass using the depth buffer's per-tile min/max, so empty clusters are skipped entirely. This is what makes the <500us budget in a shipped engine achievable.

tiled_clustered_light_culling.applicability_conditions: Pays off once the scene has enough lights that per-pixel iteration dominates. The paper locates the switch: 'the crossover point between tiled and clustered implementations is at most around 2 k lights'.
tiled_clustered_light_culling.limitations: Clustering itself costs time and memory and grows with resolution and depth slices; at very low light counts plain tiled is cheaper ('0.24 ms' tiled vs '0.71 ms' clustered at 32 lights). All the timings in the source are from a 2012 research implementation on period hardware. Cluster lists interact with transparency, which typically has to fall back to a simpler path.
tiled_clustered_light_culling.required_data_and_tools: A depth buffer with per-tile min/max, a cluster light-list buffer, and a GPU profiler able to time the light-assignment pass at the target light count.

impact.gpu: high at large light counts (17 ms vs 97.1 ms in the paper's scene; binning held under 500 us in a shipped engine)
impact.vram: medium (per-cluster light index lists; grows with lights x clusters)

tiled_clustered_light_culling.quality_impact: None: it is a culling method, not a shading change. It is what makes hundreds of lights affordable in the first place.
tiled_clustered_light_culling.concept_impact: Changes the light budget from 'a handful' to 'hundreds', which changes how levels can be lit and authored.
tiled_clustered_light_culling.recommended_stage: vertical_slice, with the real target light count. Choosing tiled vs clustered on an unrealistic light count leads to the wrong choice.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d cluster build pass + 5d shading integration + 4d light-list memory tuning + 5d validation at the target light count and on the min-spec GPU; p80 = round(1.6 * p50).

relations.note: Clustered and tiled are the light-assignment strategies for deferred and forward+ respectively; the paper measures both.
Culling raises the ceiling; a priority budget keeps the worst case bounded.
Fewer visible objects means smaller cluster lists; both are GPU-driven culling.
Light assignment depends only on depth, so it is a good async-compute candidate.

tiled_clustered_light_culling.verification: Time the lighting pass at the target light count on the min-spec GPU, and confirm the light-assignment pass stays inside its budget (a shipped example holds binning to <500 us).

portal_scene_capture_budget.problem: A portal that shows another place in real time means rendering the scene at least one extra time per portal, into a texture, from a virtual camera. Cost is therefore multiplicative in the number of visible portals and the recursion depth.

implementation_variants.name: Screen-space UV sampling of a screen-sized render target
implementation_variants.description: Render the virtual camera into a full-screen render target, then on the portal surface use the fragment's screen position as the UV: 'We use the screen-space position of each pixel on the portal surface as a UV coordinate on the screen-sized image captured by the virtual camera'. Cheaper to extend to recursion than a stencil approach.

implementation_variants.name: Stencil-buffer masking of the portal region
implementation_variants.description: 'we've been using the stencil buffer to cut portal holes in the image texture captured by the main camera, then applying the virtual camera's texture over the holes as a post-processing effect'. The author reports it becomes 'cumbersome having to deal with multiple stencil ID values' once recursion is added.

implementation_variants.name: Recursion by rendering iterations in reverse order
implementation_variants.description: 'we must capture the iterations in reverse - the deepest iteration is done first and the texture applied to the portal, then the second-deepest iteration is performed with the texture from the deepest iteration applied to the portal surface'. The reference implementation uses 'private const int iterations = 7' and two ping-pong targets.

implementation_variants.name: Reduced-resolution portal targets with upscaling
implementation_variants.description: Render each portal iteration at half or quarter resolution and upscale when compositing. Directly trades portal sharpness for a quadratic reduction in the extra render cost.

implementation_variants.name: Scissor/stencil-rect restriction to the portal's screen area
implementation_variants.description: Only rasterise the pixels the portal can actually occupy. In the reference implementation the stencil is retained for exactly this: 'We aren't using the stencil for portal rendering - we're using it to correctly cull parts of the portal outline.'

portal_scene_capture_budget.applicability_conditions: Only pay the cost when a portal is actually visible: the reference implementation checks 'portals[0].IsRendererVisible()' before running the loop. Requires oblique near-plane clipping so geometry between the camera and the portal plane is not captured.
portal_scene_capture_budget.limitations: The cost model is brutal: N visible portals x D recursion depth extra scene renders, plus one screen-sized render target per portal. The reference implementation allocates 'new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 24, RenderTextureFormat.ARGB32)' twice - full resolution, 24-bit depth, uncompressed ARGB. Recursion also has to be captured deepest-first, which serialises the passes. NOTE: no Epic primary page could be verified this pass (SRC-RND-037 is 404), so engine-specific scene-capture cost guidance is absent.
portal_scene_capture_budget.required_data_and_tools: A virtual camera with oblique near-plane clipping, a pool of render targets, portal-surface visibility tests, and CPU/GPU measurement on entering a portal.

impact.cpu: high (a full extra cull+submit per portal iteration)
impact.gpu: high (a full extra scene render per visible portal per recursion level)
impact.vram: medium to high (one screen-sized colour+depth target per portal; two at full resolution in the reference implementation)

portal_scene_capture_budget.quality_impact: High when it works - it is the only way to see through a portal convincingly. Reduced-resolution and low recursion depth are the two quality knobs that make it affordable.
portal_scene_capture_budget.concept_impact: Enables portal/non-Euclidean mechanics, but forces the whole rest of the frame budget to be halved or quartered, which constrains every other rendering decision.
portal_scene_capture_budget.recommended_stage: prototype: a portal mechanic must be proven with the real frame budget before level design commits to it.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d virtual camera + oblique clipping + 4d recursive capture loop and target pooling + 5d visibility/recursion culling + 7d budget work (resolution, depth, per-platform); p80 = round(1.6 * p50). No published effort figure.

Both multiply the number of scene renders; split screen + portals is the worst case for the frame budget.
DRS can absorb the portal cost dynamically instead of dropping quality permanently.
A depth prepass makes each extra portal render cheaper by removing overdraw.
Volumetrics are computed per view; each portal iteration pays for another froxel volume unless shared.

splitscreen_render_budget.problem: Split screen means rendering N independent views in the frame time previously available for one. Every per-view cost - culling, shadow rendering, GI, volumetrics, post - is paid N times.

implementation_variants.name: Two full viewports with reduced per-view resolution and quality
implementation_variants.description: Each view gets a smaller viewport and a reduced quality setting. Hazelight's Lead Programmer states the constraint plainly: 'the graphics side is always a challenge, since we need to render both players' views at the same time, which imposes more limitations. This demands good communication between tech and art to find creative solutions.'

implementation_variants.name: Scalability tier drop while split screen is active
implementation_variants.description: Epic names split screen explicitly as a reason scaling exists: 'Modern games need to run on a wide range of hardware and need to adapt the game performance for various needs, such as split screen or some special gameplay mode.'

implementation_variants.name: Share scene-wide work across views (shadows, GI, volumetrics)
implementation_variants.description: Where the two views overlap in the world, compute expensive scene-wide data once and reuse it for both cameras. Requires the system to tolerate a view that is not the one the data was built for.

implementation_variants.name: Alternate views across frames at half rate
implementation_variants.description: Update each player's view every other frame. Cheapest possible option; halves effective responsiveness and is only acceptable for slow-paced gameplay.

splitscreen_render_budget.applicability_conditions: Only relevant when N>1 views must be presented simultaneously on one GPU. Requires the renderer to support multiple viewports/scissor rects and per-view camera state without a full state rebuild.
splitscreen_render_budget.limitations: Nearly every GPU system is per-view, so the saving has to come from resolution and quality, not from clever sharing, unless the engine was designed for it. Hazelight also flags a second, non-graphics cost: 'Networking is always an extra challenge for us. A lot of the usual shortcuts don't really work when you can see the other players screen as well.'
splitscreen_render_budget.required_data_and_tools: Per-viewport GPU timing (a GPU capture that can attribute cost to each viewport), a thread-bound/render-thread breakdown, and per-view scalability overrides.

impact.cpu: high (N x culling and submission; the render thread is usually the first wall hit)
impact.gpu: high (N x per-view passes; mitigated only by lower per-view resolution)
impact.ram: low to medium (N sets of view-dependent state)
impact.vram: medium (N viewports' worth of intermediate targets unless shared)
impact.network: medium in co-op (Hazelight notes replication shortcuts stop working when both screens are visible)

splitscreen_render_budget.quality_impact: Each view is visibly lower fidelity than the single-player mode. This is a product-level trade-off, not a purely technical one.
splitscreen_render_budget.concept_impact: Determines whether local co-op is viable at all on a given target hardware, and it constrains the whole art budget rather than one system.
splitscreen_render_budget.recommended_stage: prototype: local co-op must be prototyped with the real frame budget before content is built for it.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d multi-viewport rendering support + 5d per-view scalability overrides + 6d shadow/GI/post sharing or reduction + 8d per-platform tuning; p80 = round(1.6 * p50). No published effort figure; expert_estimate.

Both multiply scene renders; the combination is usually unaffordable.
Post is per-view, so it is the first place to cut when splitting.

meshlet_pipeline_adoption.problem: The classic vertex pipeline re-reads and re-processes index data for every draw and cannot cull or amplify geometry without writing a new index buffer to memory. Meshlets plus mesh/amplification shaders move that work into a programmable compute-like stage.

implementation_variants.name: Amplification shader + mesh shader (full replacement of VS/HS/DS/GS)
implementation_variants.description: Microsoft: 'VS, HS, DS, and GS shader stages are replaced with Amplification Shader and Mesh Shader. Roughly, Mesh shaders replace VS+GS or DS+GS shaders and Amplification shaders replace VS+HS.' Geometry must be refactored: 'Mesh shaders require developers to refactor their geometry toolchain by separating geometry into compressed batches (meshlets) ... and turn off hardware index reads altogether.'

implementation_variants.name: Mesh shader without an amplification shader (fully ordered rasterisation)
implementation_variants.description: Dropping the AS restores a total order: 'If the pipeline state includes a mesh shader but no amplification shader, the outputs of each thread group are retired by the rasterizer sequentially with respect to neighboring thread groups.' With an AS 'only partial ordering of rasterization output is guaranteed'. Any ordering-dependent effect (blending, ROVs) cares about this.

implementation_variants.name: GPU-driven rendering with meshlets (shipped example)
implementation_variants.description: Remedy's Northlight: 'a new GPU-driven rendering pipeline' using 'mesh shaders' with 'single-pixel occlusion precision' and 'meshlet culling'. This is the practical reason to adopt the pipeline - the culling granularity, not the shader stage itself.

implementation_variants.name: Vertex-shader fallback path built from the same meshlet data
implementation_variants.description: Microsoft explicitly supports the migration: 'Titles can convert meshlets into regular index buffers for vertex shader fallback.' This is how a project can adopt meshlets while keeping older hardware or a fallback tier.

meshlet_pipeline_adoption.applicability_conditions: D3D12 or Vulkan (VK_EXT_mesh_shader) only: 'The Amplification shader and the Mesh shader are only supported for D3D12.' Requires an offline meshlet build step in the asset pipeline, and hardware that exposes the feature. On Vulkan the limits are device-queryable rather than fixed.
meshlet_pipeline_adoption.limitations: Hard caps per threadgroup: 'X*Y*Z <= 128' threads, 'Mesh shader max output verts 256', 'Mesh shader max output prims 256', mesh output '<= 32,768' bytes with the attribute packing limit 'vert_attr_bytes * ALIGN32(n_verts) + prim_attr_bytes * ALIGN32(n_prims) <= 32,768', amplification payload '<= 16k' and the two combined 'must not exceed 47k'; groupshared is 'reduced to 28k' for mesh shaders vs 32k for amplification. DispatchMesh requires 'Each of the three thread group counts must be less than 64k and the product ... must not exceed 2^22'. Index buffers and input layouts are gone: 'With Mesh shaders, index buffers and input layouts can not be specified in the PipelineState description.' Streamout is not carried over. Some hardware limits SV_RenderTargetArrayIndex to 'a 3 bit value ... at most 8 render targets'. Most importantly, Khronos is explicit that this is not automatic: 'Mesh shaders are not necessarily a performance win compared to the existing pipeline ... that cost is likely platform dependent.'
meshlet_pipeline_adoption.required_data_and_tools: An offline meshlet builder, a GPU-driven submission path (indirect dispatch), a profiler that can time the geometry stage separately, and - per Khronos - the ability to A/B against the classic path on every target platform.

impact.cpu: medium to high reduction in draw submission when combined with GPU-driven rendering
impact.gpu: unknown to medium - Khronos states mesh shaders are 'not necessarily a performance win'; the benefit is workload-dependent and must be measured
impact.disk: low to medium (meshlet data is a build artefact)

meshlet_pipeline_adoption.quality_impact: Enables much higher geometric density and per-meshlet LOD, which is a visible quality win; no direct shading-quality change.
meshlet_pipeline_adoption.concept_impact: A prerequisite for a fully GPU-driven renderer. It is an architecture change, not an optimisation: it touches the asset pipeline, the culling system and every material.
meshlet_pipeline_adoption.recommended_stage: preproduction for a new renderer; for an existing renderer, only after a measured A/B shows a win on every target platform.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 12d offline meshlet build + 10d amplification/mesh shader authoring + 8d culling integration + 15d A/B validation across vendors and a fallback path; p80 = round(1.6 * p50). Khronos requires per-platform A/B, which is why validation dominates.

gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.problem: Even after frustum culling, most submitted geometry is invisible: it is back-facing, behind other geometry, or smaller than a pixel. Culling at meshlet granularity on the GPU removes it before rasterisation instead of after.

implementation_variants.name: Frustum + backface culling in the amplification shader
implementation_variants.description: The amplification shader decides how many mesh shader groups to launch: 'The Amplification shader allows users to decide how many Mesh shader groups to run and passes data to those groups.' Culling at this level removes whole meshlets with no per-vertex work.

implementation_variants.name: Per-meshlet occlusion culling against a depth hierarchy
implementation_variants.description: Remedy's shipped pipeline achieves 'single-pixel occlusion precision' with 'meshlet culling', i.e. the test is fine enough to reject meshlets that occupy less than a pixel rather than merely testing a bounding box.

implementation_variants.name: Cluster-hierarchy LOD selection (Nanite-style)
implementation_variants.description: Choose a meshlet LOD by projected error so the pipeline never processes more triangles than the screen can resolve. Requires a cluster hierarchy built offline and a streaming system for it.

implementation_variants.name: Cone/backface culling per meshlet using a precomputed normal cone
implementation_variants.description: Store a normal cone plus a bounding sphere per meshlet and reject the whole meshlet when the cone is back-facing. Cheap (a few bytes per meshlet) and independent of any depth buffer.

gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.applicability_conditions: Requires meshlet data with bounds (and ideally a normal cone) built offline, and a GPU-driven submission path. The benefit scales with geometric density: sparse scenes gain little.
gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.limitations: Culling itself costs time, and small meshlets reduce the efficiency of both culling and shading. The mesh shader output caps (256 verts / 256 prims, 32k bytes per threadgroup) constrain how much work one group can emit. Culling against last frame's depth creates one-frame latency artefacts on fast camera moves. Vulkan's extension leaves the limits device-queryable and warns the result is 'likely platform dependent'.
gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.required_data_and_tools: An offline meshlet builder emitting bounds/normal cones, a GPU profiler that can report surviving primitives after culling, and a test scene with known occlusion density.

impact.cpu: low to medium (less work submitted when the pipeline is GPU-driven)
impact.gpu: medium to high reduction in vertex and raster work for dense scenes; no absolute figure verified - Khronos states mesh shaders are 'not necessarily a performance win'
impact.vram: low to medium (bounds/cone data per meshlet)
impact.disk: low to medium (meshlet metadata in the build)

gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.quality_impact: Indirect but large: the density that culling makes affordable is directly visible.
gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.concept_impact: Turns geometry cost into a function of what is visible rather than what is submitted, which changes what level art can do.
gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.recommended_stage: vertical_slice with representative density; measure surviving primitives before committing.

effort_person_days.formula: p50 = 6d meshlet bounds/cone build + 6d AS culling implementation + 5d occlusion integration + 7d measurement of surviving primitives and per-GPU tuning; p80 = round(1.6 * p50).

relations.note: Per-meshlet culling requires the meshlet pipeline; Khronos notes that without a measured win the pipeline itself may not pay off.
Meshlet bounds are tested against the same Hi-Z pyramid used for object-level occlusion.
Surviving meshlets are only cheap if they can be drawn without per-material state changes.
No verified source measures meshlet culling on an async queue.

gpu_meshlet_culling_budget.verification: Count surviving primitives and time the geometry pass before and after culling, on a scene with representative density; verify no visible popping from one-frame-latency depth tests.
